item.title: Lil Baby Plans Charity Shift Toward Jobs And Schools After Millions In Giveaways
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Lil Baby's next charity plans focus on jobs and schools, building on years of giveaways and a $150,000 scholarship fund.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Baby plans to steer his nonprofit toward jobs and school support, telling Jaylen Brown he wants the millions he spends on Atlanta giveaways to have a lasting effect on young people.

In “The Last Ten,” released October 16 by Glass Window Productions, he said he told his team “this year is my last time doing that” while discussing his back-to-school and Christmas drives.

Lil Baby wants to work directly with schools and school boards, create “real jobs” and give young people places to go. He used $100,000 as an example of money that could change a system once he understood how it worked.

He wants young people to still point to the help 20 years later. Brown agreed, urging people with money and influence to change the systems that leave families in need.

His current giving includes the sixth annual Back to School Fest, which served 4,000 Atlanta students on July 25 at West End Production Park.

Lil Baby and The Jones Project provided free school supplies, clothing, uniforms, haircuts, food and gift cards, WSB-TV reported.

Families also had games and other activities, with support from partners including The Athlete’s Foot, Fanatics and Dr. Bombay.

At the festival, Lil Baby spent the day meeting children and parents. His earlier community work also includes fixing up basketball courts at Oakland City Park, donating shoes, bicycles and winter coats, and helping pay students’ college tuition.

Education has been part of that work for years. In March 2020, he announced a $150,000 endowed scholarship fund at Booker T. Washington High School, which he once attended. The “My Turn” awards were meant for students who showed excellence and leadership in class.

Atlanta Public Schools officials said the first scholarship went to a senior bound for Dartmouth College, where he planned to play football. The amount of that first award was not disclosed.

At the 2025 festival, Lil Baby explained that a lack of shoes and school supplies could steer children off track. He also spoke about sparing parents the stress of paying for those things.

He said he is already working on the new approach, but did not announce school partners or a launch date.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Diddy’s Lawyers Want Out After Seven Months Without A Payment
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Diddy's law firm sought to leave another rape case, citing seven months without payment amid his documentary and prison disputes.
item.content:encoded:
Diddy faced another bid by his lawyers to drop him after they told a federal judge he had paid them nothing for more than seven months.

Sher Tremonte LLP asked to withdraw from Thalia Graves’ sexual assault lawsuit in an October 15 filing, extending a fee dispute that had already spilled into other cases. Partner Michael Tremonte also sought permission to hold Diddy’s files until the firm received its money.

The declaration did not disclose the amount owed. It said Diddy, whose legal name is Sean Combs, last paid for work and expenses dating to late 2025.

“More specifically, Mr. Combs has not paid Sher Tremonte anything for over seven months and his last payment related to fees and expenses that were incurred in late 2025. Accordingly, a substantial portion of the total overdue balance consists of invoices that are over 90 days in arrears,” Tremonte wrote.

The firm said the problem went beyond money. Tremonte accused Diddy of refusing the direct talks needed to handle his cases, despite repeated warnings sent to Fort Dix and to the person holding his power of attorney.

“In addition to Mr. Combs’s refusal to pay in accordance with the express terms of his agreement to do so, there has been a total breakdown in cooperation and communication between Mr. Combs and the Firm. Mr. Combs has declined to make himself available for timely, substantive, and direct communications about his cases for over four months,” he wrote.

Graves sued Diddy and Joseph Sherman in September 2024, alleging they drugged and raped her at a New York recording studio in 2001 and recorded the assault. Diddy denied her allegations. Sherman denied ever meeting her.

The new request followed Sher Tremonte’s attempts to leave Diddy’s cases involving producer Lil Rod and NewsNation parent Nexstar. In September, Diddy disputed the firm’s billing through spokesperson Juda Engelmayer, telling USA TODAY that lawyers had charged him for work he never approved. He described the split as a business dispute.

That fight over his own legal bills came as Diddy was also ordered to cover an opponent’s costs in his documentary battle.

On October 6, Judge Phaedra F. Perry-Bond awarded NBCUniversal, Peacock and Ample $477,700.50 after dismissing his lawsuit over Diddy: The Making of a Bad Boy. Diddy had sought at least $100 million, alleging the film spread false accusations involving murder and sex with minors. The judge cut the companies’ requested legal bill of $990,292 by more than half.

NBC also put his prison life under scrutiny. Its September investigation cited former fellow inmates who alleged he had access to liquor and banned electronics and paid others for meals, cleaning and massages. His team maintained he was following prison rules.

Union official Jose Rojas told TMZ Diddy’s record listed July 31 and September 30 fights, plus phone violations.

NBC separately reported that prison officials sanctioned him for disruptive conduct and stripped him of 41 days of good-conduct time, citing a union official.

The latest prison controversy also brought a firm denial. The Bureau of Prisons told USA TODAY on October 15 that the reported fight with Christopher “Dudus” Coke did not happen. Engelmayer said Diddy’s team had no verified information that anyone attacked him or that he suffered injuries.

Diddy is serving a 50-month sentence after his convictions on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution. He was acquitted of racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking.

In the Graves case, Tremonte argued that replacing counsel would not delay a trial or hearing because the case was stayed while two appeals addressed the law underlying a dismissal argument. The firm asked the judge to approve its exit and let it retain the files until payment.

item.title: Doechii Producer Stoic Isn’t Sold On ’90s Boom-Bap
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Stoic connected his selective boom-bap taste with a simpler studio process and a stronger voice when guiding artists through songs.
item.content:encoded:
Stoic explained why much of 1990s boom-bap left him cold, even as he praised some of the producers who helped shape it.

The producer behind Doechii’s “Bullfrog,” from her Grammy-winning Alligator Bites Never Heal, discussed his taste and growing confidence in a new interview with Hearing Things.

“I’m admittedly not the hugest fan of ’90s boom-bap beats,” he said.

His exceptions included Q-Tip, J Dilla and Madlib. He singled out A Tribe Called Quest’s “Electric Relaxation” for its restrained drums, bassline and uncluttered arrangement.

Stoic also argued No I.D. deserved more consideration in top-10 and even top-five producer conversations. He praised how Jay-Z’s “The Story of O.J.” transformed a sample while giving the rapper something to play against.

The choices accompanied a more assertive approach to his own sessions.

“I feel comfortable being in a room and guiding a song now,” he said, contrasting that confidence with his approach five or six years earlier.

That preference for room inside a beat carried into his own work. Stoic said the project file for “Bullfrog” contained roughly five tracks, with drums, bass and guitar forming its core.

He described keeping the middle of a mix clear for vocals, then placing other sounds around that space. Drums and bass anchored the track while textures and higher sounds gave it color. He had learned to picture a recording room where musicians occupied separate areas, rather than piling every instrument together.

His tools followed the same principle. He limited his main collection to roughly 20 favorite plugins and sounds, allowing him to work with fewer choices and finish tracks more efficiently.

Stoic took the same approach when selecting beats for his producer album PAELLA!. He chose tracks that left enough room for rappers, acknowledging that producers could add too much simply because they enjoyed the process.

His usual method began with a drum break and a sample. After finding and arranging roughly eight to 12 useful pieces, he removed the original break and built his own drums. Bass or guitar could follow.

He also mixed while composing. Rather than relying on an elaborate chain, he said equalization, volume levels and panning accounted for about 95% of his mixing work.

item.title: Drake Sued Over “Janice STFU” By Songwriter Behind Beyoncé’s “Heated”
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Drake’s former collaborator took a dispute over demo files, songwriting credit and the chorus of “Janice STFU” to federal court.
item.content:encoded:
Drake faced a copyright lawsuit from a former collaborator who alleged the rapper copied his demo’s chorus for “Janice STFU” and had his lawyers demand that the songwriter stop claiming credit.

Songwriter and producer Aviel Calev Hirschfield, known professionally as GoodbyeCalev, sued Drake, OVO Sound LLC, UMG Recordings Inc. and Universal Music Publishing Inc. in California federal court on October 16.

GoodbyeCalev alleged the idea began when he heard Lykke Li’s “I Follow Rivers” during a drive to Seattle. With Drake in mind, he developed lyrics and a melody over an instrumental supplied by production duo FNZ.

According to the complaint, he finished recording around January 25, 2026, then sent the demo to FNZ and other Drake collaborators. He said he received no reply and first heard the released song around May 15.

“Janice STFU’s chorus is literally identical to the Copyrighted Work in lyrics, melody, and cadence,” the complaint alleged.

GoodbyeCalev said his manager supplied recording stems and metadata to support his claim. However, he alleged Drake’s representatives maintained the rapper wrote the chorus independently and suggested GoodbyeCalev had manipulated the files’ metadata.

“Such a deception would constitute career suicide by Avi,” the filing stated, using his nickname.

He also alleged Drake’s lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter demanding he stop publicly claiming he wrote the chorus.

Billboard, which first reported the lawsuit, said a Drake representative declined to comment. UMG representatives did not immediately respond to the publication’s request for comment.

The disagreement followed an established songwriting connection. GoodbyeCalev and Drake shared writing credits on Beyoncé’s “Heated,” from her 2022 album Renaissance.

In a 2023 Willamette Week interview, the Portland producer described learning that Beyoncé had picked up a track his manager circulated. The success allowed him to reinvest in his studio after years working as a rapper, producer and engineer.

“Janice STFU” arrived on Iceman on May 15. Its interpolation of Li’s 2011 song had already drawn attention, but GoodbyeCalev’s complaint centered on the eight-line chorus he alleged he created for Drake.

The song became a major hit. Billboard reported that it spent two weeks atop the Hot 100 and 20 weeks at No. 1 on Hot Rap Songs, Drake’s longest reign on the latter chart.

GoodbyeCalev requested damages, profits attributable to the alleged infringement and a jury trial. He did not specify a dollar amount in the complaint.

item.title: Lil Wayne Concert Derailed Three Hours Before Showtime
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Lil Wayne's Charleston concert was postponed hours before showtime after weather and travel delays, with no new date announced.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Wayne had to put his Charleston fans on hold Friday after weather and travel delays derailed his concert just hours before showtime.

The Charleston Coliseum and Convention Center postponed the October 16 stop on his “20 Years Of Carter Classics” tour. The West Virginia venue had scheduled doors for 7 P.M. and the performance for 8:30 P.M. Eastern. WCHS placed the announcement just after 5:30 P.M., leaving roughly three hours between the notice and the planned start.

No replacement date had been announced. The venue’s statement said tickets already purchased would remain valid when the show was rescheduled. Updates would appear on its website and go directly to ticketholders by email.

The notice blamed “inclement weather and travel delays” without identifying a flight, airport or particular storm. It also did not announce that other stops would be postponed. The tour’s next listed performance was Saturday at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio.

Charleston had been on the calendar since March, when Lil Wayne extended his Carter celebration into another year. The venue advertised 2 Chainz as its special guest. Live Nation promoted the larger run as a celebration of more than two decades of the Tha Carter series, with 2 Chainz joining most dates and The Game appearing at select shows.

The new delay followed an earlier disruption on the same tour that eventually ended with Lil Wayne returning to perform. He missed the June 30 show in Bangor, Maine, after 2 Chainz had already played his set. Fans waited roughly two hours after the opening set, until around 11 P.M., before learning the headliner would not appear. Lil Wayne later explained that a severe migraine had put him at risk of a seizure that night. Charleston’s notice cited weather and travel rather than a health problem.

Lil Wayne subsequently apologized and returned to Maine Savings Amphitheater on July 28. The Bangor Daily News covered that makeup performance and reported that tickets from the original night were honored. He apologized again when he took the stage.

The Charleston venue said, “More information will be posted here and emailed to ticketholders directly when available.”

item.title: Gunna And Walmart Pledge $10,000 In FAMU Student Scholarships
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Gunna’s run club will join FAMU’s homecoming 5K as five students in health-related majors receive $2,000 scholarships.
item.content:encoded:
Gunna’s Wunna Run Club and Walmart pledged $10,000 in scholarships as part of a new link with Florida A&M University’s homecoming 5K. The school announced the partnership on October 16, pairing its annual race with aid for five students.

Each student will receive $2,000. The awards will go to students whose majors have a health-related component, FAMU said.

The October 22 event at Bragg Memorial Stadium will be the fifth annual Walmart-sponsored homecoming run and walk. FAMU said it has drawn hundreds of people. Walmart’s Regine Moore said the company’s goal had been “showing up consistently for a community we genuinely value.”

The partnership followed more than a year of Wunna Run events. Gunna announced the club in August 2025 before its first major 5K in Brooklyn. He hosted that race at Prospect Park on September 3. Organizer NYCRUNS handled registration, timing and the course, turning the artist’s fitness project into a staffed public event. NYCRUNS said the Brooklyn race reached its registration limit within hours of the signup opening.

The club also held runs in Houston and Toronto. It later reached Johannesburg, where Gunna hosted another 5K in January.

Gunna explained the club’s appeal to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. He said the response pushed him to keep going because people had come together for something other than a concert.

“It was for a run, and it was all community,” he said. “My vision is coming to life.”

His Atlanta run this year was set to benefit Gunna’s Great Giveaway, his nonprofit serving families in South Fulton. He also said his own fitness routine had taught him to balance studio time with training and helped his stamina onstage. He said he often used runs to listen to beats or songs he had just made. Time away from the studio gave him a chance to think through changes before he went back to work.

FAMU’s homecoming runs from October 18 through October 25. The 5K was already on the calendar before Friday’s announcement added Wunna Run Club and the scholarships. Runners and walkers must register in advance, with signup closing at noon Tuesday, October 20.

item.title: Cardi B Lands Billboard Canada’s First Global Woman Of The Year Award
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Cardi B will return to Toronto for a new global honor after an arena run that put her among the world's top touring acts.
item.content:encoded:
Cardi B will receive Billboard Canada’s first Global Woman of the Year award at its Women In Music event in Toronto on November 24.

The organizer announced her selection Friday, October 16. She will accept the honor at Rebel, six years after she won Billboard’s U.S. Woman of the Year title. The announcement credits her with 46 songs on the Canadian Hot 100, including eight top 10 hits.

The nod also follows a strong year on the road. Pollstar’s midyear report ranked Cardi seventh among the world’s top touring acts, with a $72.1 million gross from her Little Miss Drama Tour.

That run took her through North American arenas from February through April. By the tour’s halfway point, she had sold 209,622 tickets across its first 17 shows and grossed more than $32 million.

She toured behind her second album, Am I the Drama?, which came out in September 2025. The new award brings her back to Canada after that arena run included stops in Vancouver, Toronto and Hamilton.

She also sold out two shows at the Forum in Inglewood, a first for a female rapper, her tour promoter said.

Her first Woman of the Year honor came in 2020, when “WAP” with Megan Thee Stallion spent four weeks atop the Hot 100. That December, the ceremony took place virtually during the coronavirus pandemic.

At the 2020 show, she tied the honor to how her work had grown. “I want to be the best I can at anything that I do,” she said. “There’s hope for your dreams.”

That earlier honor recognized her music, live shows, cultural reach and activism throughout the year.

Her first Grammy came in 2019, the year before her first Billboard honor. She became the first solo woman to win Best Rap Album, taking the prize for her debut, Invasion of Privacy. Her career tally now stands at one win and 11 nominations. “Outside” earned her a Best Rap Performance nod in 2026.

The Toronto event will also honor Live Nation Canada’s Melissa Bubb-Clarke as Executive of the Year. Kristy Fletcher of MusiCounts, CARAS and the Juno Awards will receive its Impact Award.

Tickets for the November 24 event are on sale.

item.title: Young Thug’s YSL Trial Headed To Netflix?
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Young Thug's judicial ordeal gains a Hollywood dimension as a forthcoming Netflix production promises unprecedented scrutiny of the YSL prosecution.
item.content:encoded:
Young Thug‘s sprawling Georgia racketeering case could become the subject of a new Netflix documentary titled “Young Thug on Trial,” reportedly scheduled for 2027.

The proposed production would revisit one of the most closely watched criminal proceedings in Hip-Hop history, a case that brought questions about rap lyrics, artistic expression and the criminal justice system into the national spotlight.

However, the reported Netflix announcement and 2027 release date still require independent confirmation. No filmmakers, interview participants or production details have been established from the information provided.

The project has now received a significant confirmation from someone directly involved in the case.

Fulton County Superior Court Judge Paige Whitaker, who presided over the trial, discussed the documentary during an interview published Oct. 13 on Class E’s “What You Need to Know” program.

“Netflix and Passion Pictures are doing a documentary of the YSL trial,” Whitaker said. “I was interviewed for that documentary and it is supposed to air sometime next year.” 

The judge also indicated that an exclusivity agreement limits what she can discuss before the documentary premieres.

According to published reports, the approximately 90-minute production will be directed by Shianne Brown, with Kari Lia and Hamish Fergusson serving as executive producers. The film is expected to explore Young Thug’s rise from Atlanta’s music scene and the prosecution’s allegations that YSL operated as a criminal street gang.

The underlying case began in 2022 when Young Thug, whose legal name is Jeffery Williams, was indicted alongside other defendants under Georgia’s racketeering statute.

The proceedings became notorious for their extraordinary length, courtroom disruptions and disputes over the introduction of rap lyrics as evidence. Prosecutors argued that certain lyrics helped establish connections to alleged criminal activity. Defense attorneys challenged the implications of treating artistic expression as evidence of wrongdoing.

Young Thug ultimately entered guilty and no contest pleas in October 2024. His sentence allowed him to leave custody subject to 15 years of probation and other conditions.

The forthcoming film will not be the first documentary to examine the case. ABC News Studios released “Rap Trap: Hip-Hop on Trial” in 2023, examining the prosecution and the broader debate over criminalizing rap lyrics. 

Still, Whitaker’s participation gives the new production a potentially valuable perspective from inside the courtroom.

No precise premiere date has been disclosed, and Netflix has not independently confirmed the complete release details in the official materials I located.

For Young Thug, the courtroom proceedings may be over, but their consequences continue to shape his public story. The next chapter will unfold before a streaming audience, revisiting a legal battle that forced Hip-Hop to confront how its words can be interpreted far beyond the recording studio.

item.title: IShowSpeed Joins Obama-Backed “The Eyes Of Ghana” As Producer
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: IShowSpeed joined an Obama-backed Ghana documentary as a producer, helping promote a film about saving endangered archives.
item.content:encoded:
IShowSpeed joined “The Eyes Of Ghana” as a producer, helping promote the Obama-backed film’s one-night theater release to his audience.

Breakwater Studios and Higher Ground announced the new partnership earlier this week. The streamer shared the trailer for the October 28, 2026, event across the United States and Canada. He received a producer credit under Darren Watkins, while Barack and Michelle Obama served as executive producers.

The new film credit extended his media work beyond livestreaming. He had also bought a Miami-area warehouse to build a content studio.

Director Ben Proudfoot’s film centers on Chris Hesse, the Ghanaian cameraman who filmed his country’s independence and kept its images safe for decades. Hesse worked for Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first president. After Nkrumah’s overthrow in 1966, he protected more than 1,300 reels that recorded African independence and visits by world leaders.

“I’m humbled by his legacy and proud to help bring his story to my community,” Speed said of Hesse in the announcement.

The film had screened at festivals in 2025. Speed’s new role put his reach behind this year’s theater push.

The work went well beyond the footage that reached the screen. Earlier this year, Proudfoot told Ghana’s national broadcaster, GBC, that the film used about 15 minutes from the archive. He estimated that more than 300 hours of original negatives remained in a London vault.

Proudfoot warned that age and chemical decay threatened the footage. He called on government bodies, cultural groups and international partners to help save it.

Filmmaker Anita Afonu explained why she wanted the images back in Ghana.

“Our work is to bring them home to the people they belong to, and home is Ghana,” she told The Produced.

The negatives had gone to London because Ghana lacked the facilities to store them, Afonu said. She wanted people in Ghana to have digital copies. As a film student, she had studied European, Soviet and Hollywood work while films by earlier Ghanaian directors stayed out of reach.

The documentary also follows the restoration of Accra’s Rex Theater as a place to show Hesse’s work. Afonu told the Hawai‘i International Film Festival that she hoped the film’s success would draw support for the full archive.

item.title: Chad Hugo Fires Back At Pharrell Over Nearly 50 Neptunes Sessions
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Chad Hugo challenged Pharrell's dismissal bid with claims about studio work, missing records and disputed song credits.
item.content:encoded:
Chad Hugo fired back at Pharrell Williams’ bid to toss his copyright case, citing nearly 50 studio sessions from 2019 through 2021.

According to Rolling Stone, Hugo said Pharrell and music firms held records he needed to name released songs. He said he sought books and royalty statements from 2021 through 2024 but got almost nothing.

“Defendants ask the court to write Chad Hugo out of The Neptunes on the pleadings, before a single document has been produced,” the filing said, Rolling Stone reported.

Hugo cited EarthGang’s “U Gotta.” He claimed his name was dropped from its credits even though the artists said he helped make it.

Pharrell moved on October 6 to throw out claims he argued left the songs and rights unclear. His lawyer, Edwin F. McPherson, said Hugo should name the works he claimed to have helped make.

“They are asking that he simply identify what ‘works’ he claims to have co-authored. This is exclusively within his own knowledge,” McPherson argued in the earlier filing.

In an earlier version of the suit, Hugo named eight works and left room for other music. Pharrell’s lawyers argued that the open-ended claims left them unable to tell which songs or recordings he meant.

Pharrell’s role was central to how the track was pitched to the public. EarthGang’s PR firm, twnty three, called “U Gotta” a Pharrell-produced record in its October 30, 2024 release for “Perfect Fantasy.” It also named him as the featured guest.

The U.S. Copyright Office explains that a song’s music and lyrics are protected separately from its recording, and those rights can have different owners and licensing deals. Pharrell’s demand for clarity therefore reached two questions: which works Hugo claimed, and which rights he said he owned in each.

Hugo also sought the books for The Neptunes and N.E.R.D. to learn what he was owed. He claimed he had not been fully paid for the band’s 2017 album “No One Ever Really Dies.” Hugo alleged that his missing pay for that album could reach $1 million.

Pharrell’s lawyers did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone’s request for comment.
